## Suit for Partition and Temporary Injunction

SUIT FOR PARTITION, DECLARATION OF SHARE, PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY INJUNCTION

The Plaintiff above-named submits as under:

## Facts of the Case

1. That the Plaintiff is the adopted daughter of Late [Deceased Father's Name] and the Defendant, [Name of Mother]. The Plaintiff has no siblings. The parties are Hindus and are governed by Hindu Law.

2. That the Plaintiff's adoptive father, Late [Deceased Father's Name], passed away intestate approximately 5 years ago, leaving behind the Plaintiff and the Defendant as his only Class I legal heirs.

3. That during his lifetime, the deceased father of the Plaintiff was the absolute owner of two residential flats situated in Pune, the full particulars of which are described in the Schedule of Property annexed hereto and hereinafter referred to as the "Suit Properties".

4. That upon the demise of the Plaintiff's father, the Plaintiff and the Defendant, being the sole legal heirs, succeeded to the Suit Properties jointly and have been in joint possession thereof. The Plaintiff and Defendant are each entitled to an equal, undivided one-half (1/2) share in the Suit Properties.

5. That recently, the Defendant's behaviour towards the Plaintiff has become hostile. The Defendant has been attempting to dispossess the Plaintiff from the family home and has explicitly threatened to transfer the Suit Properties to her cousin, thereby depriving the Plaintiff of her rightful and legitimate share.

6. That the Plaintiff's name has not yet been mutated in the official property records, and the Defendant is taking undue advantage of this fact to illegally and wrongfully exclude the Plaintiff from her inheritance.

7. That the cause of action arose recently when the Defendant threatened to dispossess the Plaintiff and alienate the Suit Properties. The Plaintiff demanded her share, but the Defendant has refused to partition the properties, necessitating the filing of the present suit.

## Legal Provisions

8. That the parties to the suit are Hindus, and the succession to the estate of the deceased is governed by the provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

9. That the Plaintiff, being the adopted daughter, has all the rights and privileges of a natural-born daughter in the adoptive family. As per Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, an adopted child is deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the date of the adoption.

10. That as per Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property of a Hindu male dying intestate devolves upon the heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule. The Plaintiff (daughter) and the Defendant (widow) are the only Class I heirs of the deceased.

11. That consequently, the Plaintiff and the Defendant are each entitled to an equal one-half (1/2) share in the Suit Properties left by the deceased.

12. That in light of the Defendant's attempts to create third-party rights and alienate the Suit Properties, it is imperative to grant a temporary injunction restraining the Defendant, her agents, or anyone acting on her behalf from selling, transferring, mortgaging, or creating any third-party interest in the Suit Properties pending the final disposal of this suit, as provided under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

## Plaintiff's Entitlement and Share

13. That the Plaintiff submits that as the legally adopted daughter of the Late [Deceased Father's Name], she is conferred with all the rights and obligations of a natural-born daughter. By virtue of Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, from the date of adoption, all ties of the child in the family of her birth are severed and replaced by those created by the adoption in the adoptive family.

14. That upon the intestate demise of her adoptive father, the Plaintiff, being his daughter, and the Defendant, being his widow, are the only surviving Class I heirs as specified in the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

15. That in accordance with the rules of succession laid down in the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Plaintiff and the Defendant are entitled to succeed to the Suit Properties simultaneously and in equal measure. Therefore, the Plaintiff has a clear, vested, and indefeasible right to an equal, undivided one-half (1/2) share in the Suit Properties described in the Schedule hereto. The Defendant's attempt to deny this share is contrary to law and equity.

## Grounds for Temporary Injunction

16. That the Plaintiff has a strong prima facie case in her favour, as her entitlement to a one-half share in the Suit Properties is established by the unambiguous provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Defendant has no legal right to deny the Plaintiff's share or to deal with the entire property as her own.

17. That the balance of convenience lies overwhelmingly in favour of granting the temporary injunction. If the
injunction is not granted, the Defendant is likely to act upon her threats to sell or transfer the Suit Properties,
which would create third-party interests and lead to a multiplicity of legal proceedings. This would cause immense
hardship to the Plaintiff. Conversely, granting the injunction would cause no prejudice to the Defendant, as it would
only preserve the properties until the rights of the parties are finally adjudicated by this Hon'ble Court.

18. That the Plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the injunction is not granted. The Defendant has explicitly threatened to dispossess the Plaintiff and alienate the properties to her cousin. If the Defendant succeeds in creating third-party rights, the Plaintiff will be wrongfully deprived of her rightful inheritance and shelter. Such a loss cannot be compensated in monetary terms.

19. That it is therefore just, equitable, and necessary in the interest of justice that this Hon'ble Court be pleased to grant an ad-interim temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, restraining the Defendant, her agents, servants, or any person claiming through her, from alienating, encumbering, transferring, or creating any third-party rights in respect of the Suit Properties during the pendency of this suit.

## Jurisdiction and Valuation

20. That the Suit Properties are situated in Pune, which is within the territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court. Therefore, this Hon'ble Court has the jurisdiction to entertain, try, and dispose of the present suit.

21. That for the purposes of court fees and jurisdiction, the suit is valued as follows:
a. For the relief of partition and separate possession, the suit is valued at the market value of the Plaintiff's one-half (1/2) share in the Suit Properties, which is estimated at Rs. [Value of Plaintiff's Share]. The appropriate court fee as prescribed under the Maharashtra Court Fees Act, 1959, is paid herewith.
b. For the relief of injunction, a separate valuation is not required as it is an ancillary relief.
The Plaintiff undertakes to pay any additional court fee that this Hon'ble Court may direct upon a precise determination of the value of the properties.

## Prayer

It is, therefore, most humbly and respectfully prayed that this Hon'ble Court may be pleased to:

a. Pass a preliminary decree declaring that the Plaintiff is entitled to an equal, undivided one-half (1/2) share in the Suit Properties, more particularly described in the Schedule of Property annexed hereto.

b. Pass a final decree for partition of the Suit Properties by metes and bounds and put the Plaintiff in separate, vacant, and peaceful possession of her one-half (1/2) share.

c. Pass a decree of permanent injunction restraining the Defendant, her agents, servants, assigns, or any person claiming through or under her, from selling, transferring, alienating, mortgaging, encumbering, or creating any third-party rights or interest in any manner whatsoever in respect of the Suit Properties.

d. Grant a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, restraining the Defendant, her agents, servants, assigns, or any person claiming through or under her, from selling, transferring, alienating, mortgaging, encumbering, or creating any third-party rights or interest in the Suit Properties during the pendency and final disposal of this suit.

e. Award the costs of this suit to the Plaintiff from the Defendant.

f. Grant any other and further relief as this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.

## Verification

I, Rupa D/o. Late [Deceased Father's Name], the Plaintiff above-named, do hereby verify that the contents of paragraphs 1 to 21 of the foregoing plaint are true and correct to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief, and that nothing material has been concealed therefrom.

Verified at Pune on this ______ day of __________, 2024.

(Signature of Plaintiff)
Rupa

## REFERENCES & CITATIONS


### LEGAL_CONCEPTS CITATIONS:
## Medical Negligence

Medical negligence arises when a medical professional or healthcare provider deviates from the accepted standard of care, resulting in injury or harm to a patient. The standard of care refers to the level of skill and care that a reasonably competent medical professional in the same field would exercise under similar circumstances. To establish medical negligence, four elements must generally be proven:
-   **Duty of Care:** The medical professional owed a duty of care to the patient.
-   **Breach of Duty:** The medical professional breached that duty by failing to meet the accepted standard of care.
-   **Causation:** The breach of duty directly caused the patient's injury.
-   **Damages:** The patient suffered actual damages as a result of the injury.

Medical negligence claims in India are primarily governed by the principles of tort law and can also be pursued under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, where medical services are considered "services" provided to a consumer.

## Partition Suit

A partition suit is a legal action initiated in a civil court to divide jointly owned property among co-owners. The purpose of such a suit is to ensure that each co-owner receives a distinct, legally recognized share, leading to clear title, full ownership, and exclusive possession of their respective portion. Partition can be achieved mutually through a partition deed or, in the absence of an agreement, by filing a civil suit.

The governing legal frameworks for partition in India depend on the religion of the co-owners and the nature of the property:
-   **Hindu Succession Act, 1956:** This is the primary law for Hindus, Jains, Buddhists, and Sikhs, governing inheritance and division of property, particularly in Hindu Joint Families.
-   **Indian Succession Act, 1925:** Applies to Christians and Parsis.
-   **Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937:** Governs property division for the Muslim community.
-   **Transfer of Property Act, 1882:** Provides foundational legal principles for property transfer applicable to all citizens.
-   **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908:** This procedural law governs the entire process of filing and adjudicating a partition suit.

Any co-owner who is unable to reach an amicable agreement on property division can file a partition suit.

## Temporary Injunction

A temporary injunction is an interim order issued by a court to maintain the status quo or prevent harm to a party during the pendency of legal proceedings. Its purpose is to protect the party seeking the injunction from potential irreparable damage while the case is being resolved and to preserve the subject matter of the dispute.

The rules and provisions governing temporary injunctions are detailed in Order XXXIX of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
-   **Order XXXIX, Rule 1:** Allows the court to grant an injunction to prevent a breach of an obligation or harm arising from a legitimate fear of such a breach, especially if property is in danger of being wasted, damaged, alienated, or wrongfully sold, or if a defendant threatens to remove or dispose of property or commit a breach of contract or other injury.
-   **Order XXXIX, Rule 2:** Provides for injunctions to restrain the continuance of a breach of contract or injury of any kind.

The court considers the following three essential conditions before granting a temporary injunction:
-   **Prima Facie Case:** The applicant must present a case with sufficient merit, indicating a reasonable chance of success at trial.
-   **Irreparable Injury:** There must be a risk of harm that cannot be adequately remedied through monetary compensation alone.
-   **Balance of Convenience:** The court must assess whether the harm to the applicant from not granting the injunction outweighs any potential inconvenience to the other party.

## Adopted Daughter Property Rights

Under Indian law, particularly for Hindus, an adopted daughter enjoys significant property rights, largely equivalent to those of a biological daughter.

-   **Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA):** Section 12 of HAMA stipulates that an adopted child is deemed to be the child of their adoptive father or mother for all purposes from the date of adoption. From this date, all ties of the child in their birth family are severed and replaced by those created by the adoption in the adoptive family. An important exception is that the adopted child is not deprived of any estate vested in them prior to their adoption in their natural family.
-   **Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005):** With the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, gender
discrimination in property inheritance was abolished. Adopted daughters now enjoy equal rights as coparceners in
ancestral property and have the same inheritance rights for self-acquired property, regardless of gender. This means an
adopted daughter receives an equal share of ancestral property, just like an adopted son. An adopted daughter, even
after marriage, retains her right in the ancestral and self-acquired property of her adoptive family.

Children legally adopted under HAMA or the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, are considered on par with biological children regarding inheritance rights.

## Civil Liability vs Criminal Cheating

The distinction between civil liability and criminal cheating primarily lies in the element of 'intention' or *mens rea* and the nature of the wrong.

-   **Civil Liability:**
    -   Deals with private disputes, such as breach of contract, money recovery, or property disputes.
    -   The primary objective is to compensate or restore the aggrieved party for the loss suffered.
    -   It concerns private rights (*rights in personam*).
    -   A mere breach of contract, without fraudulent intent from the inception, typically leads to civil liability.

-   **Criminal Cheating (Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860):**
    -   Deals with offenses considered injurious to society at large, where the State prosecutes the accused.
    -   The primary objective is to punish the offender.
    -   It concerns public wrongs (*rights in rem*).
    -   The crucial differentiator for criminal cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, is the presence of dishonest intention (*mens rea*) from the very beginning of the transaction. If the dishonest intention develops subsequently due to commercial failure or breach, it generally remains a civil breach and does not constitute criminal cheating.
    -   Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, punishes cheating with dishonest inducement, carrying a potential punishment of up to seven years imprisonment and a fine.

A single act can sometimes lead to both civil and criminal proceedings, as courts allow both cases to run separately due to their different objectives and standards of proof.

## Consumer Protection Act 2019 Defective Product Liability

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, introduces comprehensive provisions for product liability, holding manufacturers, sellers, and service providers accountable for defective products or deficient services.

-   **Definition of Product Liability:** Section 2(34) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, defines "product liability" as the responsibility of a product manufacturer or seller of any product or service provided to compensate for loss or harm caused to any consumer due to any defect in the product manufactured or sold, or any deficiency in the service provided.
-   **Scope:** Product liability laws protect consumers by holding manufacturers, distributors, suppliers, and retailers accountable for the safety of their products. This includes liability arising from defects in design, manufacturing, or marketing (e.g., failure to provide adequate warnings or instructions).
-   **Strict Liability:** The Act imposes strict liability on manufacturers of defective products for harm caused by those products. This means that consumers injured by defective products can sue for compensation without necessarily having to prove that the manufacturer was negligent; it is sufficient to prove that the product was defective and that the injury or damage was caused by the product.
-   **Establishing Harm:** To bring a product liability action, a consumer must establish that 'harm' was caused due to a 'defective' product. The Act distinguishes between the roles of a product manufacturer, product seller, and service provider, with individual criteria for attracting product liability actions against each.

## Admissibility of Electronic Evidence Section 65B Indian Evidence Act

Sections 65A and 65B were inserted into the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, in 2000, following the enactment of the Information Technology Act, 2000, to address the admissibility of electronic records.

-   **Section 65A:** Provides special provisions for evidence relating to electronic records, stating that their contents may be proved in accordance with Section 65B.
-   **Section 65B:** Governs the admissibility of electronic records.
    -   **Sub-section (1):** States that any information contained in an electronic record (printed on paper, stored, recorded, or copied in optical or magnetic media produced by a computer) shall be deemed to be a document and admissible as evidence without further proof or production of the original, provided the conditions mentioned in the section are satisfied.
    -   **Sub-section (2):** Lays down conditions regarding the computer output, such as the computer being in regular use for storing or processing information for the activities of the organization.
-   **Sub-section (4):** Requires a certificate identifying the electronic record, describing the manner of its
production, particulars of the device involved, and affirming that it was produced in the ordinary course of business.
This certificate must be produced by a person occupying a responsible official position in relation to the operation of
the device or management of relevant activities. The Supreme Court has clarified that this certificate is a mandatory
condition precedent for the admissibility of electronic evidence if the original electronic record cannot be produced as
primary evidence.

**Landmark Judgments:**
-   *Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer, (2014) 10 SCC 473*: The Supreme Court clarified that the certificate required under Section 65B(4) is mandatory for the admissibility of electronic evidence.
-   *Arjun Panditrao v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal & Ors., (2020) 7 SCC 1*: A three-judge bench of the Supreme Court provided further clarity, reiterating the mandatory nature of the Section 65B(4) certificate when the original electronic record is not produced as primary evidence.

## Anticipatory Bail

Anticipatory bail is a pre-arrest bail granted by a court to a person who apprehends arrest on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence. It is incorporated under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

-   **Purpose:** The primary purpose of anticipatory bail is to protect an individual's liberty and prevent false implication in fabricated cases, ensuring they are not subjected to unnecessary detention before trial.
-   **Jurisdiction:** An application for anticipatory bail can be made to either the Court of Session or the High Court, both having concurrent jurisdiction.
-   **Conditions for Grant:** The grant of anticipatory bail is at the sole discretion of the court, which exercises this discretion based on sound judicial principles. The apprehension of arrest must be based on reasonable grounds, not mere flimsy or vague grounds.
    Common conditions imposed by the court while granting anticipatory bail include:
    -   The person shall make themselves available for interrogation by the investigating officer as and when required.
    -   The person shall not tamper with the evidence or influence witnesses.
    -   The person shall not leave the country without the prior permission of the court.
    -   The person shall not commit any similar offence while on bail.
    -   The person may be required to furnish a bail bond.

The court considers factors such as the nature and gravity of the accusation, the antecedents of the applicant (e.g., whether they are a habitual offender), and the likelihood of the applicant fleeing justice. Filing of a First Information Report (FIR) is not a pre-condition for invoking Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
